heard: There's nobody driving this car, so how does it see you? In 2004, not one robot car could finish a desert race. This year, Waymo passed half a million rides a week, with nobody at the wheel. First, the car has to see you. On its roof, LiDAR fires laser pulses and times each bounce, building a 3D picture of the street. Radar tracks speed even in rain, cameras pick out traffic lights and signs. But seeing isn't enough, it guesses where the people, bikes and cars around it might go next. Then it plans a path around all of them, again and again as they move. Waymo has practiced over 20 billion miles in simulation. Tesla bet differently, cameras only, no LiDAR, and one neural network that turns video into driving. Tesla's people buy still need a driver watching, but some Tesla robotaxis in Texas now run with no employee on board. So is it cracked? Not yet, but in parts of about 15 US cities, a car with no driver already sees you, guesses your next step, and drives around you.
